reason: The hypothesis relies on the thermal stability and sintering resistance of Pt on high-entropy supports (E1, E2), the activity enhancement upon thermal aging (E1), and the durability under hydrothermal conditions (E2). However, the cited evidence involves Pt nanoparticles on a high-entropy oxide support, not trace Pt segregation in a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy, and the poisoning-resistance premise is supported only by DFT calculations on doped Pt(111) for methanol oxidation (E3), not by experimental data for CO oxidation in automotive exhaust with H2O and NO. premises: Pt nanoparticles on a high-entropy oxide (HEO) support exhibit exceptional thermal stability and sinter-resistance due to the high-entropy effect.
Thermally aged Pt/HEO catalysts show improved CO oxidation activity (lower T100) compared to the fresh catalyst.
Pt/HEO catalysts maintain consistent CO oxidation activity over hundreds of hours and show ignorable performance decline under hydrothermal cycling with water vapor.
Doping Pt with elements like Bi or Sn weakens CO binding on adjacent Pt sites, suppressing CO poisoning.
